Abstract
The river flow, sediment transport, bed deformation and contaminant transport are strongly 
coupled under the impacts of climate change and anthropogenic activities. Two-dimen-
sional (2D) mathematical models are practical tools for predicting the morphodynamic pro-
cesses and contaminant transport while their computational efficiency is a key impediment 
to simulations featuring large scales of time and space, especially when refined meshes are 
required for key spot such as hydraulic structures. Therefore, a computationally efficient 
and fully coupled 2D model for sediment-borne contaminant transport is established under 
the framework of Finite Volume Method on unstructured meshes in this paper. The com-
puting strategies of local time stepping, parallel computing and high performance clusters 
are employed, which can speed up the computation and reduce the run time drastically. The 
model is tested against three experimental cases and one idealized test case, where numeri-
cal solutions are in general agreement with the measured data and analytical solution.
Keywords  Sediment-borne contaminant transport · Water quality model · Fluvial 
process · Shallow water hydro-sediment-morphodynamic model · Local time stepping ·

sediment–water interfaces have been the hotspots of nutrient transformation [4] [5]. This 
situation calls for consideration of sediment transport and bed deformation in the study of 
river water quality, especially for sediment-borne contaminants.
Mathematical models are useful tools to predict the riverine sediment-borne contami-
nant transport and then help water management as well as decision making. Sharma and 
Kansal [2] reviewed several popular river quality models, most of which treated sediment 
as an environmental element and the effects of sediment transport and bed deformation 
on contaminants were rarely incorporated [6]. James et al. [7] and Chung et al. [8] con-
sidered the sediment resuspension in water quality models while the bed deformation and 
sediment deposition were not incorporated into the model. Again, Hu et al. [9] established 
a water quality model with the effect of sediment on contaminant reflecting on a coeffi-
cient rather than directly calculating the bed erosion and deposition. Chu and Rediske [10] 
attempted to develop a model for metal and sediment transport in a coupled stream-wetland 
system; however, the model neglected the bed deformation as well as the impacts of sedi-
ment transport on fluvial flow. Shabani et al. [11] coupled HEC-RAS 2D, a hydrodynamic 
model with WASP, a water quality model, and the effects of sediment on contaminant 
were overlooked. Yet, there are studies concerning a whole process of fluvial flow, sedi-
ment transport, bed deformation and contaminant transport [12] [13, 14]. Actually, shallow 
water hydro-sediment-morphodynamic models have experienced a great development over 
the last two decades [15] and have a wide range of applications to riverine fluvial processes 
[16, 17] [18], while its coupling with contaminant transport was rarely reported. On the 
one hand, the coupling of fluvial flow, sediment transport and bed deformation is impor-
tant from the perspective of theoretical integrity to accurately predict the morphodynamic 
processes [19], i.e., the fluid shears the sediment grains to erode or deposit, giving rise to 
eclectic landforms [20, 21]; and on the other hand, the effects of sediment transport and 
bed deformation on the sediment-borne contaminant should also be considered in the water 
quality model so as to reflect the physical processes.
Although widely employed in scenarios featuring large scales of river length and simu-
lation time [10] [13, 14], one-dimensional models are too crude to reflect the details of 
sediment transport, bed deformation and then contaminant transport; and three-dimen-
sional models demand too much computing power. Therefore, two-dimensional (2D) mod-
els remain to be the preferred choice for cases featuring medium scales of time and space 
due to their reasonable balance between theoretical integrity and applicability [18, 22, 23]. 
However, the two-dimensional models have the potential of simulating large scale prob-
lems thanks to the rapid development of computer science as well as the improved numeri-
cal scheme. Park and Kuo, and Park et al. intended to accelerate the water quality model 
by a multi-step computation scheme two decades ago with a speed-up effect of about 58% 
[24, 25]. Originally, the application of unstructured meshes is motivated by the advantages 
of generating grids around complex geometries and moreover facilitating mesh refinements 
in locations demanding detailed investigation such as bridges and other hydraulic struc-
tures [26]. However, according to the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability condition, a 
small mesh size is likely to dictate a relatively small time step and hence the computational 
efficiency is drastically reduced if a global time step is utilized for the entire computational 
domain. In this connection, Osher and Sanders [27] first put forward the concept of explicit 
time differencing technique, which was later referred to as local time stepping (LTS) and 
was developed and implemented by researchers [16, 28] [29–31]. Yet, this strategy is not 
yet reported in the field of water quality modeling. Moreover, the past decades witnessed 
tremendous advancement in computer science that parallel computing and high perfor-
mance clusters were gradually applied in the mathematical modeling.

The present work aims to establish a computationally efficient model for sediment-borne 
contaminant transport, which can be used to simulate the concentration variations of the 
highly concerned nutrients such as phosphorus and nitrogen. The mathematical model is 
introduced in Sect. 2, including the governing equations, model closure and numerical algo-
rithm. Then the model is tested against three experimental cases in terms of hydro-sediment-
morphodynamic processes and one analytical solution in terms of conservative contaminant 
transport in Sect. 3. In Sect. 4, the model accuracy, efficiency and advantage are discussed, 
followed by Conclusions in Sect. 5.
2  Mathematical model
A fully coupled 2D model of fluvial flow, sediment transport, bed deformation and sediment-
borne contaminant transport is presented here, essentially extending from hydrodynamic 
model proposed in [32]. The governing equations, model closure and numerical algorithm of 
the model are briefed below.
2.1  Governing equations
The governing equations consist of the continuity and momentum equations for water–sedi-
ment mixture flow (Eqs. 1–3), the equations for sediment transport (Eq. 4) and bed defor-
mation (Eq. 5), and the equations for dissolved and adsorbed contaminants (Eqs. 6–7), all of 
which are listed below. Note that all these are depth-averaged 2D equations derived from the 
complete conservation laws in fluid dynamics. Although Eqs. (1–5) have been widely used in 
the field of river modelling [16] [17] [18], and Eqs. (6–7) are often applied in the field of water 
quality modelling [33], the coupling of morphodynamic processes and contaminant transport 
is relatively rare. The continuity and momentum equations for water–sediment mixture flow 
were previously solved analytically, and moreover, it was found that a unique law of concen-
tration prevails in the turbulent wall shear layer [34–36] [37]. Herein, the governing equations 
are solved numerically, and the effect of turbulent wall shear layer is neglected since the con-
vective processes are dominant in our study.

4  Discussion
Numerical models have the capability of producing exactly the same results for different 
runs under the same initial and boundary conditions and also for symmetric gauges in a 
symmetric geometry, which is the complete opposite for experiments. This is especially 
obvious in Sect. 3.2, where the measurements of two runs at y = 0.7 m near x = 0.1 m are 
not consistent (Fig. 5b), with one being severe erosion and the other marginal erosion; and 
time series of stages for symmetric gauges are distinct from each other (Figs. 4a and 4c). 
This not only indicates the uncertainty and randomness of the experiments, but also con-
firms that modeling dam-break flow on erodible beds are honestly challenging as men-
tioned in the beginning of Sect. 3.2. Note that the researchers conducting this experiments 
still have difficulties to reproduce a perfect computed result [58]. Fortunately, the tendency 
of bed deformation is well captured by the proposed model in this paper.
In order to applying the LTS, the numerical scheme here is sacrificed to merely first-
order accuracy since different cells are updated in different time steps. It is shown in 
Sects. 3.2 and 3.3 that first-order accuracy is enough for the modeling of sediment trans-
port and bed deformation, as well as the flow field, which is also proved in [16, 17]. How-
ever, when it concerns the contaminant diffusion as in Sect. 3.4, the influence is emerged 
where a smaller mesh is required to achieve a better accuracy, which was also reported in 
[65]. Morales-Hernández et al. [65] compared different combinations of mesh resolution 
and scheme order and found that the first-order scheme requires a finer mesh to provide 
an accurate result concerning diffusion than the second-order scheme, while the convec-
tive movement is well captured regardless of the mesh resolution. It is important to note 
that the application of LTS here is to accelerate the computation and shorten the run time. 
When the model is employed for a real case where refined meshes are required for certain 
spots while coarse meshes are acceptable for less important regions, the necessity of LTS 
will be evident, especially when the time scale of simulation is in years. The aim of this 
paper is to establish a computationally efficient 2D model for sediment-borne contaminant 
transport, achieving a reasonable balance between the model accuracy and computational 
efficiency. The convective transport remains to be the dominant form of movement for not 
only sediment but also contaminant in riverine flows rather than in lake or reservoir. There-
fore, the first-order scheme is still regarded acceptable for real cases in riverine flows.
The proposed model has the advantage of simulating the coupled fluvial processes featur-
ing large scales in space and time, especially where refined meshes are required for spots such

5  Conclusions
In this paper, a 2D coupled model for sediment-borne contaminant transport equipped with 
computing strategies including local time stepping (LTS), parallel computing is established 
under the framework of Finite Volume Method on unstructured meshes. Four case tests are 
conducted to validate the model accuracy. Three experimental cases of dam-break flows over 
fixed or erodible beds are reproduced by the model with satisfactory agreements with meas-
ured data in terms of time series of water stages and final bed profiles. The computed predic-
tions of contaminant concentration, resulting from an idealized sudden release of conservative 
contaminant into a steady and uniform flow field, are in good agreement with the exact solu-
tions. Moreover, the employment of LTS, parallel computing and high performance clusters is 
able to speed up the computation and the run time is reduced by 97% under the setting in the 
present work while the contribution of LTS is c. 50%, which is promising for the model appli-
cation to real cases featuring large scales both in time and space.

Abstract: The river flow, sediment transport, bed deformation and contaminant transport are strongly coupled under the impacts of climate change and anthropogenic activities. Two-dimen- sional (2D) mathematical models are practical tools for predicting the morphodynamic pro- cesses and contaminant transport while their computational efficiency is a key impediment to simulations featuring large scales of time and space, especially when refined meshes are required for key spot such as hydraulic structures. Therefore, a computationally efficient and fully coupled 2D model for sediment-borne contaminant transport is established under the framework of Finite Volume Method on unstructured meshes in this paper. The com- puting strategies of local time stepping, parallel computing and high performance clusters are employed, which can speed up the computation and reduce the run time drastically. The model is tested against three experimental cases and one idealized test case, where numeri- cal solutions are in general agreement with the measured data and analytical solution.
